How to read it

Each forecast is a probability that the Democrat wins, computed every day from what was public that day. The Brier score is the squared difference between that probability and the outcome (1 if the Democrat won, 0 if not), averaged over races. Lower is better: a constant 50% forecast scores 0.25, and a perfect one scores 0.

The time axis is logarithmic, so the final weeks get as much room as the first months. The dotted line marks the first day from which the Kalshi price has the lower mean Brier score on every remaining day. The solid line and the shading mark the first day from which that advantage also stays outside the 95% interval.

The bottom chart leaves out near-ties. In safe seats both forecasts are right, and the poll-only forecast is often just more extreme (for example 99.5% against the price's 96%), so a race counts only when the two Brier scores differ by at least 0.01.

Weights in the poll-and-price forecast

The poll-and-price forecast is logit p′ = wprice(h) × logit(Kalshi price) + wpolls(h) × logit(poll-only forecast), where both weights change smoothly with h, the number of days before Election Day. Here the weights are fitted once on all races, and the bands are 95% intervals from resampling races. A price weight above 1 moves the forecast further from 50% than the price itself.

How λ depends on modeling choices

Median λ, in days before Election Day, under each setting. The setting selected at the top of this tab is highlighted.

Null tests. We refit the weights once on each set of races, with no race left out, and compare the median λ with two alternatives: 200 draws in which every race receives another race's prices, and the same prices lagged by 90 days. If the prices carry timely, race-specific information, both alternatives should give a shorter median λ.

Comparison with the proposal's Senate results

The proposal's preliminary results for the 31 Senate races, next to this page's results for the same races. The two poll-only forecasts differ: the proposal's adds a national shift shared by all races and a fitted threshold c, and it measures λ against a rescaled poll-only control. This page uses a Kalman average of each race's own polls and measures λ against the poll-only forecast itself.

Race by race

How to read it

Each race has three forecasts for every day. The poll-only forecast is a Kalman-filter average of the race's polls, converted to a probability; it is 50% before the first poll. The Kalshi price is the midpoint between the bid and the ask of the Democratic contract; it is 50% before the market's first quote. The poll-and-price forecast combines the two on the logit scale, with weights that change smoothly with the number of days left.

The inflection point statistic λ is the number of days before Election Day from which the poll-and-price forecast stays closer to the outcome than the poll-only forecast on every remaining day. The Brier score and log loss give the same λ, because both rank a single forecast by its distance from the outcome. λ = 0 means the poll-only forecast was at least as close on the last day. λ = 671 means the poll-and-price forecast was closer from the first day of the window (1 January 2025), so the true value may be longer.

Before a race has a market or a poll, both forecasts are 50%, and a tie does not count as closer. In races without polls, λ is therefore set by the day the market opened, or by the start of the window if the market is older: the Senate markets opened in December 2024, and most House markets on 7 January 2026, 300 days before Election Day.
